title: Jacob's ladder (Genesis 28:10–22)
hook: a stone pillow, a stairway of angels: surely the Lord is in this place, and I knew it not
carry: god was here and I didn't know

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jacob's disguise: goat skins on his arms, and a blind father who said the voice is Jacob's, but the hands are the hands of Esau. Where did you own one small deception? Day three hundred sixty-two.

A young man is walking alone toward Haran, fast. Behind him, a brother who has said out loud that he means to kill him once their father dies. In front of him, an uncle he has never met, in a country he has never seen. He has the blessing he stole, and not much else. The sun goes down in the middle of nowhere. No inn. No town. He picks up one of the stones lying around, puts it under his head, and lies down on the ground. It's the kind of night people spend in airports, in cars, on a friend's floor after a terrible week. Not a place anyone would pick to meet God.
screen: `A BROTHER BEHIND HIM.` → `A STRANGER AHEAD.` → `A STONE FOR A PILLOW.`

segments.voice: Then Jacob dreams. In the King James Bible: "behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it." Some translations say stairway instead of ladder; translators aren't sure of the Hebrew. Either way, heaven and earth are joined, and the traffic runs both directions. Above it, God speaks, and does not scold the runaway. He repeats the promise made to Abraham and Isaac, and adds something personal: I am with you, I will keep you wherever you go, I will bring you back. The text doesn't say Jacob has done anything to earn it. He wakes up afraid, and says the line this day is built on: "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not." Then: "this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven." He sets his stone pillow up as a pillar, pours oil on it, and renames the spot. The place was called Luz. He calls it Bethel. Beth means house; El means God. House of God. Notice what made it holy. Not a temple, not a priest, not a good week. A rock in the middle of nowhere, and a man on the run. Christians have read the dream in more than one way. In John's Gospel, Jesus tells Nathanael that he will see the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man, and some Christians hear Jesus himself as the stairway between heaven and earth. Jewish tradition has its own readings of the dream. And some readers simply keep Jacob's surprise: God was here, and he didn't know.
screen: `A STAIRWAY, ANGELS GOING BOTH WAYS.` · `NO SCOLDING, ONLY A PROMISE.` · `THE STONE BECOMES A PILLAR.` · `LUZ RENAMED: HOUSE OF GOD.` · then, large: `SURELY THE LORD IS IN THIS PLACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: mark an ordinary place as holy. Settle, and breathe. Look around wherever you are: a kitchen, a bus seat, a desk, a bed. Pick one plain thing in front of you, a cup, a step, a doorframe. That's your stone. Rest your eyes on it. Think of something that happened in a place like this that mattered more than it looked. If you pray, you can say Jacob's words quietly: surely the Lord is in this place. If you don't, just let the place be more than it seems for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Bethel. House of God, in Hebrew. The name Jacob gave a stony place where he slept on the run and found he wasn't alone.
Your line: god was here and I didn't know. Today, when you walk through a door you walk through every day, touch the frame once, and remember Jacob's stone. Day three hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Christians often read Jacob's dream alongside John 1:51, where Jesus speaks of angels ascending and descending upon the Son of man, and the phrase "house of God" has long been used of churches and places of prayer.

fork.setup: you're Jacob. you wake at dawn on a stony hillside, shaking from a dream of heaven opened above you. what do you do?
options: get moving fast and try to forget it.
set up your stone pillow as a pillar and name the place.
go back home and make peace with your brother.
fork.reveal: he stands the stone up, pours oil on it, and renames the place Bethel, house of God. going home comes much later.

original.note: Hebrew: beth, house, and El, God. house of God.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jacob's ladder is a ladder, and maybe a children's toy.
what it means: a runaway sleeps on a stone and dreams of heaven joined to earth. he wakes saying God was here and he didn't know it.
what a scholar hears: the Hebrew word, sullam, may mean a stairway rather than a ladder; Luz becomes Bethel; and John 1:51 picks up the angels ascending and descending.
recall: a wonder, too hard to reach

notes: Hebrew sullam (Genesis 28:12) as a hapax legomenon, and the stairway/ramp reading with the Mesopotamian ziggurat comparison: common in commentaries; confirm the phrasing.
Bethel = beth (house) + El (God); Luz as the earlier name (28:19). Confirm.
God's promise (28:13–15) paraphrased as 'I am with you, I will keep you wherever you go, I will bring you back.' Confirm the paraphrase is fair.
Christian reading via John 1:51 (Jesus as the link between heaven and earth) is presented as held by many Christians, without ranking Jewish readings. Confirm.

The review recalls Genesis 27:22 in unquoted paraphrase ('the voice is Jacob's, but the hands are the hands of Esau'); the KJV reads 'The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau.' It is not presented as a quotation. Confirm.
'The Hebrew word is found nowhere else in the Bible' and the stairway/ramp reading are stated in the voice as widely held; a Keeper may want 'scholars generally' framing.
